name: Restore Permutation
description: An array of integers $$$p_{1},p_{2}, \ldots,p_{n}$$$ is called a permutation if it contains each number from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ exactly once. For example, the following arrays are permutations: $$$[3,1,2], [1], [1,2,3,4,5]$$$ and $$$[4,3,1,2]$$$. The following arrays are not permutations: $$$[2], [1,1], [2,3,4]$$$. There is a hidden permutation of length $$$n$$$. For each index $$$i$$$, you are given $$$s_{i}$$$, which equals to the sum of all $$$p_{j}$$$ such that $$$j \lt i$$$ and $$$p_{j} \lt p_{i}$$$. In other words, $$$s_i$$$ is the sum of elements before the $$$i$$$-th element that are smaller than the $$$i$$$-th element. Your task is to restore the permutation.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^{5}$$$) — the size of the permutation. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$s_{1}, s_{2}, \ldots, s_{n}$$$ ($$$0 \le s_{i} \le \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$$$). It is guaranteed that the array $$$s$$$ corresponds to a valid permutation of length $$$n$$$.
output_specification: Print $$$n$$$ integers $$$p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{n}$$$ — the elements of the restored permutation. We can show that the answer is always unique.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.
